documents.title: EFORT consensus on primary total hip arthroplasty

chunks.content: Introduction The value of computed tomography (CT) in preoperative planning for lower limb arthroplasty is increasingly recognised ( ). An optimally acquired CT scan facilitates precise implant sizing and positioning by enabling the creation of accurate three-dimensional (3D) anatomical models ( , ). CT has also proven valuable in supporting the customisation of intraoperative tools and cutting guides ( ). However, a variety of CT protocols is currently used for hip and knee arthroplasty, with limited agreement in the imaging parameters and body regions to scan ( ). A harmonised protocol document is needed to reduce variability, ensure clarity and consolidate imaging practices across the discipline. While low-dose imaging techniques have been proposed, no studies have yet consolidated orthopaedic CT practices, an essential step, given the current lack of clarity and alignment, which limits widespread adoption ( ). Two examples of such protocols are the Perth protocol ( ) and the imperial knee protocol ( ). The latter markedly reduced the body regions to be imaged from a continuous scan spanning the superior margin of the acetabulum to the talus ( ), to targeted segments: the femoral head, 20 cm at the knee and 5 cm at the ankle ( ). However, further progress is required in harmonising and optimising the imaging approach for pelvic and knee CT scans. This is essential to make these protocols broadly applicable across all orthopaedic companies, offering a balanced, cohesive approach grounded in best practice, without fundamentally altering or redefining existing protocols. This work aims to consolidate existing CT imaging protocols for lower limb arthroplasty, specifically hip, knee and lower limb reconstruction by outlining five consistent, best-practice orthopaedic protocols, which preserve the clinical intent of current CT imaging. Our objectives were to i) identify the scan volume that only includes surgically relevant areas, ii) optimise the CT imaging parameters for efficiency and clarity and iii) create a user-friendly unified protocol document that is easy for imaging centre staff to adopt. Methodology We conducted a comprehensive critical review of pelvic, hip and knee CT scan protocols and recommendations published in the literature, building upon prior work ( ). These protocols, often provided by orthopaedic companies, including implant manufacturers, are designed to optimise CT imaging for preoperative planning software for hip and knee replacements. These proprietary software systems rely on CT scans with specific imaging protocols to enable 3D modelling and templating, which are essential for implant sizing and positioning. A total of 17 hip and 12 knee CT scan protocols were identified. For comparison, key imaging parameters were extracted, including the body regions to scan (‘scan volume’ or area scanned top to bottom), scanner tube voltage (kV), current–time product (mAs) and slice thickness. These parameters are summarised in and . Informal consensus meetings We engaged the stakeholders (radiologists, orthopaedic surgeons, engineers, medical physicists, surgical technologists and industry experts) involved in the planning and execution of hip and knee replacement surgeries at our tertiary hospital for complex arthroplasty, to understand each personnel’s individual needs. We have used CT planning protocols from 17 different manufacturers. After collectively reviewing and analysing existing protocols, we discussed commonalities and differences in specific aspects, such as the scan volume (i.e. area scanned top to bottom) and imaging parameters. We found existing variability in CT imaging guidelines and practices, which is why we undertook this initiative. Deficiencies in the available protocols were described. Rather than replacing established protocols, our goal was to preserve clinical intent by amalgamating different documents into one, through merging common denominators in order to preserve clinical integrity. Throughout different stages of consolidating the protocols, all members of the panel participated in collaborative informal consensus meetings, where rationales and preliminary recommendations were formulated. The discussions were focused on how to best combine the essential information from the protocols into a single more effective and coherent document. We aimed to preserve the clinical rationale behind each individual protocol by identifying overlap and redundancy. An informal consensus approach ( , , , ) was chosen due to several reasons: i) faster decision-making; ii) limited high-quality evidence (e.g. on the optimal scan volume and imaging parameters) and iii) to encourage open discussions compared to more rigid voting and structured interviews. A draft document was created based on the agreed-upon principles and elements, which was circulated among all members for review. Feedback was collected through written comments and follow-up discussions, and modifications were made in multiple rounds until no major objections remained. The final document incorporates the minimum requirements and optimal standards to ensure high resolution. Agreement was reached when: All members agreed that the final document includes the essential elements for CT imaging in orthopaedics. All members agreed the protocol represents best clinical practice or is clinically robust and fully aligned with best practice standards. All members agreed the protocol could be implemented without compromising patient care or existing workflows. By limiting the scan volume and imaging parameters to what is surgically necessary, we outline five harmonised CT protocols: primary and revision protocols for the hip and knee and an additional protocol for total femoral replacement. The chosen imaging parameters and guidelines were supported by evidence in the literature and target enhanced surgical planning efficiency and accuracy. Results Deficiencies in current imaging guidelines The review of the hip and knee protocols revealed several key deficiencies and inconsistencies that may impact reproducibility and diagnostic quality. The main difference identified was in the recommended body regions of the patient to be imaged. Inconsistent terminology for common body regions was used across the companies. Some protocols referenced specific landmarks (e.g. ‘from ASIS to below the lesser trochanter’), while others used general terms (e.g. ‘pelvis’ or ‘hip’), leading to a lack of clarity and necessitating streamlining. In six hip protocols (35%), there is no mention of imaging the knee joint, so there will be missing regions in the scans, making measurements of leg length and femoral rotation impossible. Repeat imaging may be required if the initial scans are inadequate. In terms of imaging parameters, a notable number of protocols lacked complete technical parameter (kV, mAs) specifications. In the hip protocols, scan kV and tube current (mAs) were omitted in 53 and 65% of cases, respectively, while similar omissions were seen in 33% (kV) and 42% (mAs) of the knee protocols. The protocols also revealed lack of clarity on the recollimation of the CT slices (i.e. how the slices are reconstructed after acquisition). Some protocols differentiated between ‘acquisition’ and ‘reconstructed’ slice thickness, while others did not specify. The reported slice thickness values ranged from sub-millimetre resolution (0.5 mm) to as high as 5 mm. This variation may affect the accuracy of subsequent 3D reconstructions. The use of automated tube current modulation (ATCM) was sporadically documented. While some protocols specified ATCM as preferred or default, others omitted any reference to dose modulation strategies, potentially contributing to variability in radiation exposure. Overall, these deficiencies highlight the need for greater harmonisation in CT imaging protocols used for preoperative planning. We therefore outlined detailed protocols, which specify the bony regions required for surgical planning and outline the appropriate scanner settings to optimise image quality. The protocols can be adopted and set up on all current-generation CT scanners. The Supplemental material (see section on given at the end of the article) provides full details of these five protocols. Technical considerations All CT scan protocols in this work require the scanner to be operated in a spiral scanning mode, a setting found on most modern CT scanners. In this mode, the examination table moves continuously through the gantry as the X-ray tube rotates around the patient. In spiral CT scanning, a pitch must be defined. A value of 1 is recommended in all lower limb arthroplasty as it ensures that the data do not have gaps (nor any overlaps) and improves sampling of the patient’s anatomy. A slice thickness or collimation width of 1 mm has also been identified as an optimal choice for reducing image noise and providing sufficient image details (good spatial and contrast resolution) ( , ). Since the anatomy of interest is the bony regions, thinner slices are unnecessary as they increase scan time and patient dose ( ). When scanning multiple regions of the patient, it is crucial to ensure that all acquired slices have the same axial view, in other words, cross-sectional volume, such that the (x, y) coordinates are kept fixed from one slice to the next (only the z -coordinate should change along the length of the patient’s body). This ensures the relative positions of different regions remain consistent. Most new CT scanner systems allow for ATCM technology, accommodating variations in body shape. This accounts for the varied thickness of matter that the X-ray beam penetrates through; the tube current is increased in thicker and denser regions to reduce noise, whereas it is reduced in thinner patient cross sections to reduce radiation dose. Therefore, the application of ATCM ensures consistent image quality throughout the scan and has proven to reduce and optimise radiation dose ( ). It adapts to the patient’s size, constitution and bone quality. When using this feature, the scanner may prompt for a reference mAs value for an average-sized patient. It then adjusts the dose up or down based on the patient’s size, using the scout image (surview). If available, protocol-specific reference mAs values should be entered; otherwise, the scanner will calculate an appropriate value from the patient’s measurements. After data acquisition, but before the final image display, a CT convolution kernel is often used for optimised image reconstruction. This is also known as a reconstruction kernel, filter or algorithm. Depending on the anatomical application and region of interest, either a standard (soft tissue) or bone kernel may be used. The consolidated protocols all advise using a sharp bone kernel for the CT planning of lower limb replacement (e.g. B80f), as it offers improved spatial resolution compared with soft kernels ( , ). In revision hip and knee arthroplasty and total femoral replacement, patients have existing metal implants, which generate metal artefacts in the preoperative CT scans. These manifest as dark and bright streaks or sprays radiating outward from the metal components. This can significantly affect the reading of CT scans and the quality of surgical planning. For this reason, it is crucial to take appropriate measures to minimise the effect of the artefacts. This includes increasing the imaging parameters (kV, mAs) and applying metal artefact reduction (MAR) algorithms when available. Although increasing the scanner tube voltage and current results in greater radiation exposure, in revision surgery where failure rates are high, the good-quality imaging which increasing these parameters offers is crucial and can improve segmentation accuracy and, hence, the quality of planning. For this reason, a higher tube voltage is advised when imaging patients for revision surgery; both noise is reduced and metal artefacts are less prominent at a higher kV setting ( , , ). Modern CT scanners have built-in MAR algorithms. These algorithms can be applied during image reconstruction or post-processing after image acquisition. When available, it is recommended to use this feature, particularly when imaging patients for planning revision surgery. However, saving the DICOM dataset with and without the MAR filter is important. This precaution is necessary because MAR algorithms may alter data near metal edges and potentially introduce new artefacts, which could limit their clinical applicability ( , ). Noisy scans caused by highly attenuating metal prostheses pose significant challenges for standard CT imaging. Traditional CT scales cannot accommodate the full range of radiodensities associated with metals, resulting in saturation and spray artefacts. This limits the ability to conduct detailed assessments of metal objects as finer structural information and details are lost at the point where the CT scale saturates ( ). Consequently, the quality of metal segmentation is compromised. To address this issue, it is recommended that all CT scans be stored both with and without an extended Hounsfield scale. This feature captures metal HU values that exceed the standard range, preserving finer structural information and enhancing the greyscale representation. Recommendations Primary hip arthroplasty For patients undergoing first-time hip surgery, the scan volume should be split into three regions: the pelvis and proximal femur, the knees (distal femur) and the ankles. These imaging areas are sufficient as they capture the relevant landmarks for planning leg length and femoral rotation ( ). Although the CT scan is divided into three regions, it is a single scan in which three spiral series are taken simultaneously (in one run) and should not be mistaken for three separate scans. The scanner parameters recommended when imaging a native hip (100 kV, 100 reference mAs) take into account that image noise as a result of metal artefacts is kept to a minimum in primary CT scans. Thus, a reduction in these parameters does not result in the worsening of such artefacts. Some CT scan protocols reviewed in this work recommend an X-ray tube kV and mAs as low as these (e.g. Materialise and Conformis, respectively). Thus, these parameters are suggested in the least complex scenario of planning primary hip arthroplasty. In the work by Su et al. Thus, these parameters are suggested in the least complex scenario of planning primary hip arthroplasty. In the work by Su et al. ( ), radiation exposure of a low-dose CT (100 kV, 100 mAs) was compared against traditional CT (∼130 kV, 270 mAs) in the context of hip preservation surgery. They found almost a 90% reduction in radiation exposure (reducing the effective dose to as low as 1 mSv) while maintaining adequate image quality for clinical assessment and preoperative surgical planning. Hip preservation surgery aims to correct for morphological abnormalities, preserving as much bone as possible, so it is crucial to visualise complex hip deformities accurately and completely. Since the 100 kV and 100 mAs protocol has proven to deliver good-quality images to plan hip preservation surgery ( , ), selecting these parameters for 3D-CT planning of primary THA is justified. The work conducted by Huppertz et al. ( ) also defends the use of a very low effective dose pelvic CT protocol for 3D planning of THA, defined by an automatically preselected tube voltage of 100 kV and a reference tube current of 100 mAs. All CT datasets taken with different imaging protocols, including those taken with these parameters, were of reliable and satisfactory image quality; the reduction in the CT dose was not accompanied with a severe compromise in the image quality. Revision hip arthroplasty When planning revision hip arthroplasty, extending the CT scan volume to beyond the distal tip of the stem is a minimum requirement. However, the length of the revision stem is seldom known prior to surgery ( ). Traditionally, revision femoral stems are longer than the primary stem to be replaced ( , ). Therefore, visualising the full length of the implants in situ and the intramedullary femoral canal below the former implant offers fundamental information for optimal diaphyseal fixation. The fixation of revision stems is also largely guided by the anteroposterior and mediolateral bow of the femur (easily visualised on scans capturing the full femur). Therefore, considering these requirements, it is best practice and advised to have the scan running from the top of the pelvis (iliac crest) to the knee-joint line ( ). Since the radiographer conducting the scan does not know the length of the revision implant, this would be the reason to scan the whole femur. The large variability in revision femoral stem lengths ( ) means a standard length cannot be assumed and considered for the scan volume. Although in recent years, comparative studies have analysed the performance of short or primary length stems in revision THA against longer stems, the choice of prosthesis length is largely dependent on the quality of the metaphyseal bone, any previous revision, the indication for revision and the classification of the femoral deficiency ( ). Regardless of the choice, capturing the full length of the femur is essential for accurate decision-making. This will avoid re-imaging the patient due to an incomplete scan volume. Based on the review, 140 kV was commonly found to be the upper limit of the recommended kV; hence, it is advised to be used in revision cases; this is only justifiable in the revision scenario, given the comparatively greater risk of complications in this more complex surgery due to the presence of previous metalwork ( ). Regarding tube current, ATCM should be employed once again. However, a value of 140 mAs should be considered as a reference. Primary knee arthroplasty For planning a first-time knee replacement, the scan volume is reduced to include only what is surgically required in the knee scenario. As outlined in the Imperial Knee Protocol published by Henckel et al. ( ), the scan volume can be reduced to include only the femoral head, knee joint and the tibiotalar joint, which are needed for successful knee replacement planning. Since the landmarks needed for defining the mechanical axis (for limb alignment) can be found within these scan regions, we recommend capturing these three spiral series ( ). When planning a primary total knee replacement (TKR) for a patient with an existing total hip replacement, the imaging parameters and scan volume requirements remain unchanged. Complete imaging of the hip implant is unnecessary, as generally, only the centre of the femoral head serves as the proximal landmark required for limb alignment planning. When planning a primary total knee replacement (TKR) for a patient with an existing total hip replacement, the imaging parameters and scan volume requirements remain unchanged. Complete imaging of the hip implant is unnecessary, as generally, only the centre of the femoral head serves as the proximal landmark required for limb alignment planning. Limiting the scan volume ensures compliance with radiation safety principles, significantly reducing the patient’s exposure to ionising radiation ( ). The quality of the CT scan required for planning a primary knee arthroplasty is comparable to that of a hip arthroplasty. This is because visualisation of the osseous anatomy is the primary focus of both procedures, as the orthopaedic surgeons and engineers involved in the planning are not focused on the surrounding soft tissue envelope. Since both are metal-free scans, the proposed acquisition parameters for CT scanning of a native knee replicate those from the primary hip protocol (100 kV, 100 reference mAs). Compared with the hip joint, the native knee joint has less soft tissue and noise. Therefore, the interface between the two bones is more clearly defined ( ). The work by Henckel et al. ( ) has shown that a current–time product of 100 mAs is sufficient to confidently identify key landmarks at the hip joint, knees and ankles; <80 mAs and <45 mAs make it difficult to identify the femoral head centre at the hip and centre of the talus at the ankles, respectively. Revision knee arthroplasty The scan volume for planning a revision knee replacement should also include three spiral series. Compared to the protocol for a primary TKR, a larger scan volume is usually necessary, as implant removal during revision procedures often results in some degree of bone loss and damage, particularly to the epiphyseal bone ( ). Therefore, imaging both the metaphysis and diaphysis is essential to plan for a larger fixation area to enhance the stability of the revision components ( , ). Additionally, the preoperative CT scan must extend further to assess the potential need for bone allografts and longer stems ( ). As illustrated in , the scan volume may be extended proximally to the femoral isthmus and distally to the mid-tibia for more complex revision knee replacements. This ensures comprehensive visualisation and planning for effective surgical outcomes. Since metallic prosthetic components in the knee generate metal artefacts on the CT scan, a higher tube voltage and current–time product (120 kV, 120 reference mAs) is recommended for the knee region compared with the hip and ankles (100 kV, 100 reference mAs) to reduce metal noise. These imaging parameters remain even when a hip implant is present ( ). When available, MAR algorithms should be applied to the scans to address the metal artefacts and aid segmentation. The DICOM data must be saved with and without this. Total femoral replacement In rare cases involving complex lower limb reconstruction, complex hip or knee revision or extensive bone cancer excision, a total femoral replacement may be needed. The scan volume provided by the standard revision hip protocol may be insufficient. For example, if the presence of long hip and knee stems is evident, the revision hip protocol will fail to capture the entire length of the tibial components within the scan volume. An additional imaging protocol (the fifth protocol in the Supplementary material) may be necessary in such situations. This full lower limb protocol ensures imaging of the whole femur and tibia. A single continuous scan, extending from the top of the pelvis to the ankles is recommended instead of a series of scans ( ). This approach is important because minimal viable bone is often found between prosthetic components. Moreover, in knee replacements involving variable tibial component lengths, little bone may exist between the distal end of the implant and the ankles. Consequently, splitting the scan volume offers no significant benefit; the reduction in radiation dose would be negligible since the ankles are distant from dose-sensitive organs. Given the presence of large metal implants in these cases, the imaging parameters are comparable to those of the revision hip protocol. As with other scenarios, patient-specific factors, such as weight and anatomy, may need to be input into the CT scanner to calculate the appropriate mAs automatically. The extended scale option should also be used to achieve optimal visualisation and accurate segmentation of metal components (save raw axial slices both with and without this setting). If the CT scanner includes a proprietary MAR algorithm, it should be applied to minimise metal-induced noise. However, datasets should be exported with and without the MAR algorithm to assess any artefacts introduced during post-processing. Summary The main CT acquisition parameters recommended

However, datasets should be exported with and without the MAR algorithm to assess any artefacts introduced during post-processing. Summary The main CT acquisition parameters recommended for all five harmonised protocols – i) primary hip, ii) revision hip, iii) primary knee, iv) revision knee and v) total femoral replacement – are summarised in . Discussion The five protocols presented in this paper aim to harmonise and optimise the imaging scan volume and CT parameters, by consolidating already available protocols through an informal consensus. For the revision hip and knee protocols, additional measures were incorporated to minimise artefacts, such as increasing the effective energy of the X-ray beam – a justified adjustment since noisy scans may compromise diagnostic value and necessitate repetition. Other improvements included applying MAR filters where possible and using an extended CT scale. To limit unnecessary radiation exposure, all protocols recommend reducing the imaging volume to include only landmarks essential for surgical planning. A continuous scan from the top of the pelvis to the knee joint is only advised in the revision hip protocol due to the variable and extended lengths of revision femoral stems. However, we avoided prescribing fixed scan lengths for the scan volume. Existing protocols often specify ranges (e.g. 38–44 cm) based on average-sized patients ( , , ), which may be insufficient for larger patients or excessive for smaller patients. Anatomical variations necessitate flexibility rather than rigid measurement guidelines. Continuous scanning from the pelvis to the ankles is discouraged also due to its significant dose implications and is reserved for complex cases, such as total femoral replacement. The application of ATCM is endorsed across all scenarios. Rizzo et al. ( ) have demonstrated that ATCM can reduce radiation exposure by 42–44% compared to fixed tube currents while maintaining diagnostic image quality. Similarly, findings by Kalra et al. ( ) affirm the efficacy of modulation techniques. The harmonised protocols recommend the use of ATCM, as detailed in some of the reviewed protocols, to effectively balance image quality and radiation dose, using reference tube current values as benchmarks. This approach mitigates increased radiation exposure in areas with metallic prostheses, a key consideration for revision surgery ( ). Inputting patient characteristics (e.g. weight or BMI) into the scanner allows for automated tube current adjustments tailored to individual needs, enhancing personalised patient care. Data from the National Joint Registry 20th Annual Report ( ) have shown that between April 2003 and December 2022, 142,521 revision hip procedures were performed in the UK, with 5,137 re-revisions recorded. The high re-revision rates highlight the complexity of the surgery; improved and meticulous preoperative surgical planning can potentially contribute to a reduction in post-operative complications and enhanced surgical outcomes ( , , , ). The standard CT Hounsfield scale (ranging from −1,024 to +3,071 HU) may be adequate for primary hip arthroplasty planning. However, planning revision surgeries requires a higher dynamic range, which offers more detailed images by capturing finer differences in density and increases voxel value granularity ( ). Most modern CT scanners support extended CT scale reconstruction algorithms, and using these settings when available is recommended to enhance image and data quality ( ). All recommended protocols also mandate the use of the sharp bone kernel setting, which enhances edge definition and improves the visualisation of bony structures. This improved spatial resolution is crucial for accurate segmentation, enabling the creation of precise 3D models of the patient’s anatomy ( ). Since preoperative planning for hip and knee replacements focuses primarily on the osseous structures, using sharp convolution kernels is indispensable for optimising image quality. Conclusion A review of current CT scanning protocols for the hip and knee distributed by various orthopaedic companies revealed significant inconsistencies and called for harmonisation. We consolidated these protocols for i) primary hip, ii) revision hip, iii) primary knee, iv) revision knee and v) total femoral replacement, to address this unmet need. These harmonised protocols achieved through the informal consensus are designed to enhance diagnostic accuracy, streamline preoperative workflows and reduce the risk of procedural errors, by avoiding the use of many different imaging guidelines and protocols that may lead to confusion among radiographers. Our protocol document serves as a consolidation of these existing guidelines and includes all the essential requirements to successfully plan and assess lower limb replacement. chunks.content: Introduction Total joint arthroplasty (TJA), including total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and total hip arthroplasty (THA), has reported survivorship at 10 years of 95%, justifying TJA as the optimal surgical procedure for end-stage degenerative joint disease ( , ). Over 2 million TJAs are performed annually, with a predicted increase of 145% for THA and 147% for TKA within the next decade ( , ). The global rise in TJA has a predicted paralleled increase in associated complications ( ). This has necessitated an increased effort to prevent post-operative complications by identifying and addressing pre-operative modifiable risk factors ( , , ). There has been a significant increase in publications regarding malnutrition in orthopaedic surgery over the last 6 years, alluding to the importance of peri-operative nutritional assessment and optimisation in TJA patients ( ). Assessment of malnutrition is a key component in the pre-operative evaluation in TJA ( , , , ). Johnson et al. ( ) reviewed 84 315 patients and found that malnutrition was the strongest risk factor for poor post-operative outcomes in TJA. Multiple publications highlight that malnutrition results in numerous post-operative complications including but not limited to periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), aseptic loosening, periprosthetic fracture, dislocation, anaemia, prolonged length of stay (LOS), and TJA 90-day total cost, and an increase in mortality ( , , , , , ). Definition The term malnutrition, with its broad definition, has been used extensively in orthopaedic literature ( ). Malnutrition includes acute, subacute, or chronic states of nutrition with various aspects of both overnutrition or undernutrition, with or without an element of inflammation, leading to altered body composition and function ( , , ). Ultimately, there is an imbalance of macro- and micro-nutrients and energy consumption ( ). The definition and diagnosis of malnutrition are multifactorial, with no consensus regarding the methods used to screen and diagnose malnutrition in orthopaedic surgery ( , , , , ). This has hindered the standardisation of assessing and diagnosing malnutrition in TJA, although it has been suggested by the Joint Commission that pre-operative nutritional screening should be performed within 24 h of admission for patients undergoing surgery ( , , ). There have been numerous recommendations that all arthroplasty patients should undergo pre-operative nutritional assessment, but the details of what and how to assess remain debatable, with some even arguing that only patients with risk factors for malnutrition should be assessed ( , , , , ). It should not be overlooked that various aspects of a patient’s nutritional status affect the success of TJA, and knowledge regarding these aspects is essential for optimal pre-operative optimisation in TJA ( , , ). Epidemiology Due to the heterogeneity of definitions available and the lack of a gold standard in malnutrition assessment, there has been a wide range in the prevalence of malnutrition reported ( , ). The prevalence of malnutrition in the adult population has been reported to range from 15% to 60% ( ). In patients undergoing TJA, the prevalence of malnutrition has been reported to range from 8.5% to 50% ( , , , ). Nutritional evaluation A variety of methods have been proposed to diagnose and define malnutrition, including standardised nutritional scoring tools, clinical anthropometric criteria, and serological laboratory values ( , , , ). The clinical signs and symptoms of malnutrition may be subtle and often undetected until there has been severe progression of malnutrition; therefore, a combination of assessment methods has been proposed to evaluate nutritional status ( , , ). The most effective measure of nutritional status includes a comprehensive history and clinical examination in combination with laboratory serological markers ( ). Malnutrition is diagnosed when any of these assessment methods identify abnormal parameters ( ). Multiple co-morbidities, as well as the Charleston Comorbidity Index and the American Society of Anesthesiology classification, are associated with malnutrition ( , ). Increased age, a history of gastrointestinal pathology, a history of malignancy, and alcohol abuse predispose patients to an increased risk of malnutrition ( ). This highlights the holistic approach necessary for pre-operative optimisation, with the assessment of malnutrition beginning with a thorough medical history identifying co-morbidities ( , ). Standardised nutritional scoring tools There are numerous standardised nutritional scoring tools, combining subjective history and clinical assessment, with some utilising laboratory serological markers ( , , ) ( ). These tools focus more on identifying patients with nutritional deficiency as opposed to overnutrition. The mini nutritional assessment (MNA) is useful in identifying patients who would benefit from nutritional intervention and has been suggested as the first-choice nutritional scoring tool due to its association with serum albumin and LOS ( , , ). The mini nutritional assessment (MNA) is useful in identifying patients who would benefit from nutritional intervention and has been suggested as the first-choice nutritional scoring tool due to its association with serum albumin and LOS ( , , ). Ihle et al. ( ) evaluated the MNA in a prospective study on 351 TJA patients and found that inferior scores related to unfavourable LOS, post-operative mobilisation, and the incidence of adverse events. Guo et al. found the MNA useful in predicting patients with delayed wound healing, and the MNA has been reported as the most reliable of the nutritional scoring tools ( , ). Koren-Hakim et al. ( ) compared the adequacy of nutritional tools in the assessment of malnutrition in patients with hip fractures requiring TJA and found that the MNA, Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) and the Nutrition Risk Screening 2002 (NRS-2002) were adequate; however, only the MNA predicted poor outcomes such as re-admission rates and mortality. O’leary et al. ( ) reported that the MUST score, which identified patients at risk of malnutrition, predicted short- and medium-term mortality, LOS, and discharge destination for patients admitted for hip fractures. The MUST has been recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence for screening adult patients admitted to the hospital, and in 2017, it was the most commonly used nutritional screening tool used to collect data for the National Hip Fracture Database in the UK ( ). The NRS-2002 was used by Shang et al. ( ) to identify patients at nutritional risk when reviewing 1532 patients undergoing TJA, and found that those with nutritional risk were at increased risk of wound complications, surgical site infections, PJI, cardiac complications, respiratory complications, urinary complications, and had increased total cost and LOS. There is less published evidence on the use of the Peri-operative Nutrition Screen (PONS) in orthopaedic surgery; however, the PONS is a modified version of MUST ( ). Vitamin D and albumin are well-documented markers of malnutrition in arthroplasty surgery, which are utilised in the PONS ( ). Clinical anthropometric criteria Anthropometry measurements used in orthopaedic literature ( ) include body mass index (BMI), mid-upper arm circumference (MAC), calf circumference (CC), triceps skinfold thickness (TST), and suprapatellar index (SI) ( , ) ( ). Anthropometry measurements are less routinely documented in orthopaedic literature except for BMI ( , ). Abnormal anthropometric parameters have been associated with post-operative complications and increased LOS in orthopaedic surgery ( ). Anthropometric measurements are used as indirect measurements of nutritional status and should not be used to assess marginal or acute malnutrition ( ). They have the advantage of being cheap and easy to perform, with some forming part of the standardised nutritional scoring tools mentioned above ( ). The use of the TST has not been extensively reported in the orthopaedic literature for nutritional assessment ( ). Font-Vizcarra et al. found that TST was associated with the risk of infection in a prospective study of 213 patients undergoing TKA ( ). There was a 5% risk of infection and a 10% risk of infection with a TST of 3 cm and 2 cm, respectively ( ). Reduced CC and MAC are related to decreased muscle mass and loss of subcutaneous fat, with MAC more commonly utilised due to ease of use in hospitalised patients ( ). Using CC or MAC is not well-reported in TJA; however, both are included in the MNA, which has been used in identifying patients with malnutrition in TJA ( , ). SI is an anthropometric measurement used in TJA and related to BMI, although it has not been used directly as an assessment of malnutrition ( ). The distribution of adiposity has been noted to be important in determining infection risk and wound healing, especially in TKA ( ). SI is calculated by dividing the length of limb by the circumference of the limb 4 cm above the superior pole of the patella, with a ratio of <1.6 indicating a shorter and wider limb and increased soft tissue around the distal thigh ( ). Lozano et al. found that an SI of <1.6 more accurately predicted prolonged tourniquet time and increasing surgical difficulty in TKA ( P < 0.038) compared to using BMI alone ( ). Body mass index BMI is an important clinical assessment tool ( , , ). It is the most commonly used anthropometric measurement in TJA ( ). It is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by the square of height in metres ( ). The World Health Organization (WHO) has divided BMI into categories ( ) (

Lozano et al. found that an SI of <1.6 more accurately predicted prolonged tourniquet time and increasing surgical difficulty in TKA ( P < 0.038) compared to using BMI alone ( ). Body mass index BMI is an important clinical assessment tool ( , , ). It is the most commonly used anthropometric measurement in TJA ( ). It is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by the square of height in metres ( ). The World Health Organization (WHO) has divided BMI into categories ( ) ( ). The flaw in BMI is that it does not consider soft-tissue distribution or muscularity; however, assessing BMI is critical in nutritional assessment in TJA ( , ). Both low BMI (<18.5 kg/m 2 ) and high BMI (>30 kg/m 2 ) form part of the broad definition of malnutrition and are independent predictors of adverse events in TJA ( , ). Studies have further shown that different BMI classes are associated with different complications ( ). Increased BMI Obesity, defined as BMI >30 kg/m 2 , is well-documented as a significant modifiable risk factor in TJA ( ). It forms part of the overnutrition aspect of the definition of malnutrition associated with a change in body composition and often with other co-morbidities ( , ). The prevalence of obesity is rising, with more than 502 million people being diagnosed as obese, and it is predicted that more than 46% of Americans will be obese by 2029 ( , ). Obesity has been shown to be associated with osteoarthritis, especially of the knee, with the risk for osteoarthritis in obese patients reported to be four-fold higher and five-fold higher in males and females, respectively ( , , , ). The exponential increase in the rate of obesity recently has coincided with an increased demand in TJA ( , , ). By 2029, more than 55% of patients requiring THA will be classified as obese ( ). The TJA complications associated with obesity include surgical site infections, PJI, component malpositioning, component failure, revision arthroplasty, 10-year mortality, longer surgical duration, and increased LOS ( , , , , ). The odds ratios for major complications increase to 8× and up to 25× when BMI is over 40 kg/m 2 and 50 kg/m 2 , respectively ( ). This is in keeping with Zusmanovich et al. ( ), who found after reviewing 268 663 patients that these complications have a stepwise increase paralleled to increasing BMI, highlighting the importance of reducing BMI prior to TJA. The rate of PJI in the USA, although still low, at least doubled in both TKA and THA between 1998 and 2011 when comparing TJA in the obese and non-obese population ( ). This can increase by up to fourfold in morbidly obese patients ( ). The risk of dislocations, even in correctly positioned prosthesis in THA, is more than 4× higher in obese patients ( ). Increasing LOS linked to obesity is associated with other complications such as venous thromboembolism and rising health costs ( ). Every 5-unit increase in BMI beyond 30 kg/m 2 is associated with $500 higher hospital costs and $900 higher 90-day costs ( ). Although complications are associated with increasing BMI, a specific BMI cut-off prior to surgery has not been agreed upon ( ). Ward et al. found that BMI >40 kg/m 2 was an independent risk factor for complications such as acute kidney injury, cardiac arrest, infection, and revision surgery ( ). Optimising BMI to <40 kg/m 2 and/or aiming for at least 5–10 % weight loss has been strongly suggested ( , , , , , ). There is no consensus regarding the optimal weight loss strategy for pre-operative optimisation, with options including nutritional specialist consults, weight loss programmes, pharmacotherapy, and bariatric surgery (BS) ( , , , ). Non-surgical weight loss techniques have been reported to result in reduction of approximately 3 kg/m 2 ( ). BS can result in a total mean weight loss exceeding 31%, although its use in TJA remains controversial as malabsorption secondary to the procedure may lead to other complications ( , , ). BS techniques include gastric banding, Roux-en-Y, and sleeve gastrectomy ( , ). The average weight loss with the use of bariatric surgery prior to TJA is approximately 14 kg/m 2 ( ). Sax et al. ( ) reviewed national databases in the USA over a 10-year period and found that there was no significant difference in complications and outcomes between the timing and type of BS used prior to TJA. In a meta-analysis by Li et al. , statistically significant improvements in LOS, short-term complications, and operative time in morbidly obese patients undergoing BS were documented ( ). No

). BS techniques include gastric banding, Roux-en-Y, and sleeve gastrectomy ( , ). The average weight loss with the use of bariatric surgery prior to TJA is approximately 14 kg/m 2 ( ). Sax et al. ( ) reviewed national databases in the USA over a 10-year period and found that there was no significant difference in complications and outcomes between the timing and type of BS used prior to TJA. In a meta-analysis by Li et al. , statistically significant improvements in LOS, short-term complications, and operative time in morbidly obese patients undergoing BS were documented ( ). No difference in long-term complications was found, including dislocation, peri-prosthetic fracture, PJI, and revision surgery ( ). This is in keeping with the systematic review by Smith et al. ( ) , which found that BS reduces weight but does not significantly reduce complications or improve outcomes in TJA. The risk of TJA in obesity versus the risk of undergoing BS to reduce BMI requires further careful evaluation, and risk stratification may be necessary. Obese patients have surprisingly been found with paradoxical malnutrition, with deficiencies in serum albumin, vitamin D, vitamin C, zinc, thiamine, selenium, and iron ( , , ). Huang et al. reviewed 2161 arthroplasty patients for malnutrition using laboratory markers and found that 42.9% of obese patients were malnourished ( ). This highlights the point of using multiple aspects of nutritional assessment in TJA patients, as concomitant deficiencies in nutrition increase the risk of complications ( ). Decreased BMI Underweight (BMI <18.5 kg/m 2 ) has been associated with increased complication rates similar to obesity ( , ). There is less published data on the risk of underweight compared to obesity in TJA, most likely due to underweight patients representing a smaller proportion of the population ( ). In the USA, 1.5 % of the population are patients who are classified as underweight ( ). Underweight patients have been noted to have compromised immune systems and lower bone mineral densities predisposing patients to infections and fractures ( ). Underweight patients have increased odds ratios (OR) for aseptic loosening (1.62), periprosthetic fractures (1.5), and dislocation (1.8), with increased 2-year mortality ( , ). Schmerier et al. found revisions in underweight patients were more likely to be due to periprosthetic fractures and PJI ( ). Anoushiravani et al. compared underweight patients to patients within normal range BMI and found underweight patients were at increased risk for post-operative anaemia and cardiac complications which resulted in higher hospital costs ( ). This was supported by Sayeed et al. , reporting that underweight patients developed complications such as post-operative anaemia, deep vein thrombosis, increased LOS, and overall increased healthcare costs ( ). Although there is a paucity of information in the literature regarding nutritional interventions for underweight patients prior to TJA, additional nutritional workup has been suggested to identify and reverse other associated nutritional deficiencies ( , , ). Serological assessment Serological markers are not part of the diagnostic criteria for malnutrition according to American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (ASPEN) ( ). In the orthopaedic literature, serological markers have been found to predict complications, and therefore have been proposed as surrogates in assessment of malnutrition, especially in the subclinical setting ( , ) ( ). Serum albumin, prealbumin, total lymphocyte count (TLC), transferrin level, vitamin D, and zinc are often used to identify malnutrition in TJA, with albumin being the most widely used ( , , , , , , ). Assessment of haemoglobin may identify anaemia with associated micronutrient deficiencies of iron, folate, vitamin B12, and copper ( ). Any abnormal serological parameter predisposes the patient to be at risk for complications ( ). It should be noted that some of these serological markers are also negative acute phase reactants, and their interpretation should take this into consideration ( ). However, this should not distract from the fact that abnormal serological parameters such as hypoalbuminaemia have independently been found to be predictors of complications in arthroplasty surgery ( ). Hypoalbuminaemia Albumin is an essential and the most abundant protein in blood serum with many important roles. It transports a variety of fatty acids, steroids, and hormones with a half-life of 14–20 days ( , ). Albumin has a positive effect on the immune system with its involvement in antigen presentation to T-cells, lymphocyte proliferation, antibody responses, interleukin-2, and interferon-gamma ( ). Because of these multiple roles, the relationship between hypoalbuminaemia and post-operative complications such as PJI is multifactorial ( ). Hypoalbuminaemia (<35 g/L) in TJA has been reported to be associated with superficial surgical site infections, pneumonia, unplanned intubation and prolonged ventilation, higher blood transfusion rates, sepsis, and increased mortality ( , , , , ). In a retrospective study of 65 023 and 108 556 patients undergoing THA and

14–20 days ( , ). Because of these multiple roles, the relationship between hypoalbuminaemia and post-operative complications such as PJI is multifactorial ( ). Hypoalbuminaemia (<35 g/L) in TJA has been reported to be associated with superficial surgical site infections, pneumonia, unplanned intubation and prolonged ventilation, higher blood transfusion rates, sepsis, and increased mortality ( , , , , ). In a retrospective study of 65 023 and 108 556 patients undergoing THA and TKA, respectively, Fryhofer et al. found hypoalbuminaemia was a significant independent risk factor for adverse outcomes ( ). Bala et al. showed that hypoalbuminaemia is a significantly increased risk factor for pulmonary embolism, stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, acute renal failure, respiratory failure, and sepsis in patients undergoing TJA ( ). In the review by Loftus et al. , using hypoalbuminaemia or nutritional risk score (NRS) to diagnose malnutrition, it was reported that surgical site infections were the most common reported complication followed by increased LOS and increased costs ( ). Albumin has been suggested to be better than using BMI, with hypoalbuminaemia a more significant risk factor for post-operative complications than obesity ( , ). Albumin is a nutritional marker of protein–energy malnutrition (PEM) and has been associated with chronic disease but is also an acute-phase reactant ( , , , ). There are several disease states that affect albumin and pre-albumin levels including liver disease, catabolism, nephrotic syndrome, and protein-losing enteropathy ( ). In the acute phase of inflammation, the liver decreases production of albumin and pre-albumin in order to produce acute-phase reactants ( ). This needs to be taken into consideration with caution when interpreting results of albumin and pre-albumin in the presence of chronic disease states or inflammatory processes ( , ). Hypoalbuminemia is a modifiable risk factor for post-operative complications and a marker of ‘nutrition risk’, specifically PEM ( ). Once hypoalbuminemia is identified, referring to a nutritional specialist is useful, as increasing albumin can be approached with direct therapy using IV human albumin administration or indirectly with parental or enteral protein supplementation ( , , , ). Enteral nutritional supplementation has a significant amount of data proving its efficacy in reducing TJA complications ( , ). Studies where protein supplementation has been given peri-operatively, increasing daily protein intake, have resulted in fewer post-operative complications ( ). Schroer et al. ( ) found that prescribing a high-protein (100 g/day) peri-operative diet in patients identified as malnourished with hypoalbuminaemia improved surgical outcomes in TJA. Patients with hypoalbuminaemia can be referred to the relevant practitioners and optimised pre-operatively by targeting an intake of at least 1 g/kg daily ( ). Pre-albumin Pre-albumin is used as a nutritional marker with the advantage of having a shorter half-life compared to albumin (2–3 days), therefore is useful in acute nutritional state changes ( , ). There is no official value for pre-albumin level to be used as a marker for malnutrition in TJA ( ). Pre-albumin levels are affected by renal and liver function, infection, stress, and hydration status ( , ). Serum pre-albumin has been suggested not to be used specifically as a nutritional marker for PEM but rather as a measure of ‘nutritional risk’ ( ). Transferrin Transferrin is an acute-phase reactant with a half-life less than that of albumin at ±10 days ( , ). Serum levels decrease in the setting of severe malnutrition but may also be affected by renal failure, liver disease, and iron status ( , ). Transferrin, together with albumin, is utilised in the Rainey-MacDonald Nutritional Index (RMNI), used in screening for malnutrition ( , ). It has been shown to be a better predictor of outcomes than using TLC ( ). With nutritional intervention, serum transferrin has noted to improve similarly to the management of hypoalbuminaemia ( ). RMNI = (1.2 × serum albumin) + (0.013 × serum transferrin) − 6.43 ( ). Total lymphocyte count In malnourished states, PEM may negatively impact the maturation of lymphocytes, resulting in a decrease in the TLC below 1500/mm 3 ( ). Assessment of TLC can be used to support PEM; however, it is not specific ( ). TLC is a less reliable predictor of post-operative complications compared to albumin and should be used as a supplemental measurement of nutritional status ( , ). TLC has been shown to predict complications post-TJA, as abnormal serum albumin and TLC are associated with increased mortality in TJA following hip fractures ( ). Zinc Zinc is the second most abundant trace element in the body after iron ( ). There is a paucity of evidence regarding the assessment of perioperative zinc deficiency in TJA ( , ). Zinc

can be used to support PEM; however, it is not specific ( ). TLC is a less reliable predictor of post-operative complications compared to albumin and should be used as a supplemental measurement of nutritional status ( , ). TLC has been shown to predict complications post-TJA, as abnormal serum albumin and TLC are associated with increased mortality in TJA following hip fractures ( ). Zinc Zinc is the second most abundant trace element in the body after iron ( ). There is a paucity of evidence regarding the assessment of perioperative zinc deficiency in TJA ( , ). Zinc deficiency has been noted to affect the competence of the immune system, including innate and adaptive immunity ( ). Low pre-operative zinc levels (95 µg/dL) have been associated with delayed wound healing in orthopaedic surgery ( , , ). Complications arising from delayed wound healing are potentially devastating, ranging from superficial wound infections to wound dehiscence and PJI ( ). Assessing pre-operative zinc levels in TJA and providing supplementation may aid in decreasing the risk of these complications ( , , ). More research needs to be done in terms of the role of zinc and its deficiency in TJA. Vitamin D Vitamin D deficiency has been noted even in healthy populations, with a prevalence of 41.6% ( , , ). Vitamin D is essential in the homeostasis of bone, calcium, and phosphate, and its immunomodulatory effects play a significant role in both innate and adaptive immunity ( , ). According to Khoo et al. , vitamin D has been shown to have an effect on immune and cell-signaling pathways ( ). Vitamin D deficiency is associated with increased rates of PJI following primary TJA, with Maier et al. reporting that 86% of patients undergoing revision surgery for PJI had vitamin D deficiency ( , ). Traven et al. found that patients with hypovitaminosis D were more likely to have a 90-day complication, with 13% of these patients needing revision surgery compared to patients with normal vitamin D levels ( ). Additionally, these patients were more likely to experience infectious complications when compared to patients with normal vitamin D levels ( P < 0.001) ( ). Although there is limited evidence to support vitamin D as a standard marker in assessing nutritional status, vitamin D is an important modifiable risk factor in the orthopaedic setting, with the potential of correction in as little as 1 month ( , , ). Arshi et al. evaluated the costs of vitamin D supplementation prior to TKA and found that pre-operative restoration of vitamin D levels was a cost-effective way of reducing the risk of PJI in TKA ( ). Maniar et al. ( ) found that patients with hypovitaminosis D had lower pre-operative functional scores and recommended post-operative supplementation. Vitamins and other trace elements Iron is the most abundant trace element in the body, essential for haemoglobin ( ). Deficiencies in vitamin B12, folate, and iron result in anaemia, which has been associated with poor outcomes in TJA ( , ). Obese patients have also been found to be deficient in vitamin C, thiamine, and selenium, in addition to the previously mentioned nutritional markers ( ). Vitamin C alone has been noted to be an important nutritional parameter with its anti-oxidant, immunostimulant, anti-viral, and anti-bacterial properties ( , ). Simple interventions would include supplementation of iron and vitamin C ( ). The relationship between obesity and diabetes mellitus should also not be overlooked, and assessing haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) should be part of the pre-operative workup with the goal of achieving HbA1C <7 % ( , ). Management of malnutrition in arthroplasty There is no standardised approach to treating malnutrition in TJA, probably due to the broad use of the definition ( , ). Once malnourished patients are identified, they should be referred to the relevant health disciplines for treatment and pre-operative optimisation with targeted supplementation ( , , , ). This process of identifying and managing patients with malnutrition should involve a collaborative effort between the orthopaedic surgeon, primary care physician, and nutritional specialist ( ). The intervention depends on the type of malnutrition identified, as discussed previously under the relevant headings ( ). Nutritional supplementation directed at identified deficiencies improves malnutrition and reduces post-operative complications ( , ). It has been noted in previous studies that malnutrition has been underrecognised, limiting the referral to optimise nutritional status, and this needs to be improved ( ). Both trauma and non-trauma patients undergoing TJA, who have been identified for pre-operative optimisation of nutrition and received supplementation, have been shown to benefit ( ). Williams et al. (2020) report implementing a perioperative enhancement team, with screening beginning with the PONS, and patients identified as malnourished follow the high-risk nutritional pathway and are given a high-protein

). Nutritional supplementation directed at identified deficiencies improves malnutrition and reduces post-operative complications ( , ). It has been noted in previous studies that malnutrition has been underrecognised, limiting the referral to optimise nutritional status, and this needs to be improved ( ). Both trauma and non-trauma patients undergoing TJA, who have been identified for pre-operative optimisation of nutrition and received supplementation, have been shown to benefit ( ). Williams et al. (2020) report implementing a perioperative enhancement team, with screening beginning with the PONS, and patients identified as malnourished follow the high-risk nutritional pathway and are given a high-protein diet and nutritional supplements ( ). The first step in the correct management of malnutrition is adequate screening and diagnosis. Conclusion Malnutrition is a broad term that includes many abnormalities of nutritional status; however, in the orthopaedic literature, BMI and albumin are commonly used parameters to assess and address malnutrition. Understanding and identifying abnormal nutritional parameters are fundamental in the process of addressing malnutrition in TJA. Malnutrition is multifactorial, and a multidisciplinary and holistic approach is required to identify and reverse the various abnormal nutritional parameters. The ultimate goal in TJA is a successful procedure with no complications and optimising these nutritional parameters will aid in improving the success of TJA. chunks.content: Introduction During this era, when orthopaedic surgeons are being increasingly regulated and litigated against, most will agree that there are occasions when surgeons have to tread carefully between what they think is best for a patient and what is deemed ‘correct’ by regulators and lawyers. For the majority of the time most surgeons will practice evidence-based medicine, but patients are unique and there are times when standard techniques maybe not the best option for a patient. Most surgeons have the capacity to adapt their practice when they think it is necessary and go ‘off-label’. EFORT consider these issues extremely important; they are all about patient safety which is why they commissioned this appraisal in order to evaluate all aspects of these practices and to produce guidance for the benefit of patients, surgeons, manufacturers and regulators. In this article we will attempt to clarify and suggest recommendations around the issues of off-label, including discussing the mixing and matching of implants from different manufacturers in total joint arthroplasty (‘mix & match’) and commenting on ‘mismatch’. The commentary and conclusions we have made are based on an extensive literature review and consensus meetings. We have reached out to the specialist groups that represent the surgeons who we hope will eventually be guided by our conclusions, and have taken careful note of their opinions. Definitions and significance Any discussion about off-label procedures usually includes the subject of litigation, but even in the highest circles it seems that even liability has never been unequivocally defined. For the purposes of this article, we have attempted to define and explain the frequently used descriptions that are used in the context of this subject. Off-label Put simply, off-label means that the user of whatever the label has been placed on, is using it in a way that is not listed in the ‘indications for use’ (IFU) that are cited on the label. The United States (US) Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers off-label use as a utilization of a medical device or drug outside the intended scope of indications or patient group for which they had granted approval. In the UK, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) offers the advice: ‘You should use medical devices as described by the manufacturer in the instructions. Should you use the device in any other way, it’s considered “off-label” use’. Originally, the term off-label was almost exclusively used with respect to pharmaceutical products. In this article, the term will only be used in the context of arthroplasty implants and not in the context of other hardware or procedures (i.e. synthetic implants, allografts, etc.). Significance The significance of the term off-label in joint replacement, including in routine surgical practice, is that there are occasions when on-label devices are not readily available or, if available, they do not adequately meet the requirements for a particular patient. Thus, the surgeon turns to a device that they think would fit the requirements, but if the indication for which the surgeons is going to use it for is not in the IFU, it will be said that it has been used off-label. With this decision comes the risk that the implant manufacturer will not take responsibility if the device fails and the responsibility could rest with the surgeon, which could result in major consequences. Mix & match According to different dictionaries, a definition of the idiom ‘mix & match’ is to put different things (such as pieces of clothing, furniture or food) together in different ways. In medicine the term is also used when something is made up of complementary elements taken from different sets or sources. Commonly, in contemporary precision medicine initiatives, mixing and matching drugs is an important part of pharmacology in the medical treatment of diseases, but mixing adversely acting drugs is a medication error. In the context of total joint arthroplasty (TJA) in orthopaedic surgery, mix & match describes the use of components from more than one manufacturer in completing the construct. Significance Although off-label use as well as mix & match are frequently practiced in primary and revision arthroplasty, there is an increasing debate about potential medico-legal issues. Therefore, we ask the question: should surgeons, who feel they have no other alternative but to use off-label implants in high-risk patients or to mix and match when results of mixing and matching in a particular situation are equal or superior, be allowed to do so? In other words, should they change their practice simply to protect themselves from possible legal issues or should they continue a practice where their results or available evidence supports that mix & match might be best for their patients? Certainly, there are agencies, including the medical insurance agencies, competent authorities and manufacturers who argue otherwise. They suggest that if the outcome of a procedure is poor,

other alternative but to use off-label implants in high-risk patients or to mix and match when results of mixing and matching in a particular situation are equal or superior, be allowed to do so? In other words, should they change their practice simply to protect themselves from possible legal issues or should they continue a practice where their results or available evidence supports that mix & match might be best for their patients? Certainly, there are agencies, including the medical insurance agencies, competent authorities and manufacturers who argue otherwise. They suggest that if the outcome of a procedure is poor, the surgeon will be blamed for going off-label and litigation might ensue. It has even been said that surgeons could be held responsible for designing a new device if they went off-label, and doubt has been cast over the status of their malpractice insurance. It is suggested that well documented, informed consent from the patient outlining the advantages and drawbacks of such a mix & match procedure would mitigate against litigation. From it is clear that mixing and matching of components in total joint replacement continues to be practiced. Malcolm et al reported that 30% of total hip arthroplasty (THA) and 37% of total knee arthroplasty (TKA) procedures, using regular off-the-shelf implants, are performed in groups of patients outside those approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration for agreed indications. Due to increasing obesity and other comorbidities, they still expect future growth of these off-label procedures, emphasizing the need for continued medical device surveillance. Peters et al, reporting on mix & match, confirmed the practice as being contemporary in many countries, mainly involving THA, but, as demonstrated in , we found that it has also been reported in total shoulder replacement and in TKA operations where the patella from one manufacturer has been used with the tibial and femoral components of another. Mismatch The term ‘mismatch’ generally refers to a situation where components in a construct do not match each other (such as for size or shape) and are altogether unsuitable for each other. In arthroplasty, it is a special subtype of mixing and matching, such as when the size or connections of components do not fit or match each other. A potential mismatch between morphological features of hip or knee bone anatomy and implant configuration is not addressed in this review. Significance The significance for the patient and the surgical team is that they have implanted into a patient a construct where the components do not fit or in some way are incompatible. This is very likely to result in early failure of the construct and an early revision operation. Mismatch is generally a mistake. Methodological approach Inauguration workshop An inauguration workshop of the EFORT Implant and Patient Safety Initiative (IPSI) took place on 21 January 2020 with the participation of a steering group invited by the EFORT board. The steering group consisted of clinical experts, scientists, representatives from implant manufacturers, regulatory authorities and patient organizations. Also attending were representatives from European national societies and specialty societies, who were identified before the initiative commenced. During the workshop, the convenors (KT, LZ) introduced the scoping process and defined clinically relevant key questions about off-label use and mix & match with the participants within the workshop. It was agreed that the target audience for these recommendations will be primarily European orthopaedic surgeons. After this initial meeting, the clinical key questions have been translated into epidemiological topics by the convenors, a methodologist (TL) and members of the writing group (KT, LZ, PKA, KPG, JL, JPK, RGHHN). These key topics formed the basis for the search and synthesis of evidence which was used to develop an iterative consensus process to be used by clinical experts. The clinical recommendations have therefore been based on all the available evidence and clinical expertise. The sequential development steps of the practical recommendation are described in more detail in the following chapters. Evidence retrieval and synthesis In order to identify the best available evidence for the clinical topics, a systematic literature search was performed. Based on the information provided from the inauguration workshop, the convenors and members of the writing group defined relevant terms for the systematic literature search, which was then performed by the methodologist. Two in-depth literature searches were performed: (1) to identify available evidence for off-label use of regular implants during THA/TKA ( ), (2) to identify publications concerning the mixing of implants from different manufacturers for primary and revision THA/TKA ( ). Both literature searches were performed in EMBASE via Ovid and MEDLINE via PubMed. The titles and abstracts were screened independently in a double-blind manner by two reviewers (clinical experts) for eligibility. The search was completed by a hand search of abstracts additionally referring to the above topics. All eligible full

systematic literature search, which was then performed by the methodologist. Two in-depth literature searches were performed: (1) to identify available evidence for off-label use of regular implants during THA/TKA ( ), (2) to identify publications concerning the mixing of implants from different manufacturers for primary and revision THA/TKA ( ). Both literature searches were performed in EMBASE via Ovid and MEDLINE via PubMed. The titles and abstracts were screened independently in a double-blind manner by two reviewers (clinical experts) for eligibility. The search was completed by a hand search of abstracts additionally referring to the above topics. All eligible full texts were screened by at least two reviewers and allocated to the clinical topics. Based on the results of the systematic literature searches, the convenors and writing group members drafted a first set of recommendations for the clinically relevant topics, which served as the basis for next steps in the consensus process. For each resulting recommendation, the available evidence was summarized. Consultation of steering group, national and specialty societies In order to receive additional input from clinical experts, the writing group distributed the preliminary set of recommendations and background information to the steering group as well as to EFORT National Member Societies and Specialty Societies (National Delegates and Presidents of Specialty Societies). They received a copy of the preliminary recommendations together with the summarized evidence and were asked for comments, specifically with regard to the relevance and completeness of the recommendations. Furthermore, the national society representatives were asked to compare ‘our’ guidelines with their own national guidelines to demonstrate any shortcomings or discrepancies. A total of 26 steering group members, 70 national delegates and three specialty societies representatives were contacted and we received 40 responses (40%). Consensus voting Convenors and writing group members integrated the comments from the steering group and the national and specialty society representatives into the draft of preliminary recommendations. After confirming any possibility of potential plagiarism could not have occurred, updating references and correcting the English, the document was resent to all members of the steering group and the national and specialty society representatives to prepare consensus voting. Prior to the annual EFORT congress, a final meeting of the steering group was organized on 23 June 2021 in Dresden. The convenors presented the results of the set of recommendations with the underlying evidence to all 30 panel members who could participate. Due to the restrictions imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic only three steering group members attended the meeting in person whilst the other 27 panellists participated online. After explanation of the voting rules and voting process, consensus voting was performed. Due to the lack of a generally accepted definition of consensus in the development of recommendations, we adopted the stepwise approach as implemented during the previous consensus initiative on periprosthetic joint infections. The following levels of consensus have been established: No consensus: less than 60% agreement in the voting panel Weak consensus: 60% to 65% agreement Consensus: 66% to 74% agreement Strong consensus: 75% or more agreement Unanimous: 100% agreement During the voting process, all recommendations were displayed on a screen and the delegates were asked to vote in real time. Where necessary, the recommendations were rephrased and re-voted on. There were three possible responses to each recommendation: agree, disagree, or abstain. The voting results were communicated to the panellists electronically immediately after each vote was taken. Distribution of the consensus document Immediately after the consensus meeting, the voting results were added to the final recommendation document and the manuscript submitted for publication. When the recommendations are finally published, they will be sent to national societies as well as specialty societies who will be encouraged to distribute them to their members. In addition, the recommendations will be published on the EFORT and on individual member societies’ websites. However, in spite of it being acceptable to offer TJA in the way that is now practiced, implant labelling has largely remained unchanged, typically reflecting historic indications and contraindications. Some manufacturers still only list in their IFU primary and secondary osteoarthritis in skeletally mature individuals as a result of non-inflammatory degenerative joint disease as the indication for use. They then go on to include disorders predisposing to infection and implant loosening (i.e. obesity, metabolic disorders, osteoporosis) besides non-compliance and inadequate fixation as contraindications. Malcolm et al calculated a national off-label prevalence of 30.4% and 37.0% for THA and TKA, respectively in their United States Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project. They attributed the slight predilection for off-label practice in TKA compared to THA to higher rates of obesity (15.3% vs. 9.8%) and metabolic/bone disease (23.7% vs. 19.4%). It was also reported that with increased incidence of comorbidities the off-label rate rose annually for each procedure type during the investigated decade. Liu et al, in a single-institution study, evaluated the incidence and outcomes between patients with implants used on- and off-label. They found that, by current definition, of the 225 patients surveyed (92 hips and 133 knees), 154 patients (68.4%) had off-label implants. It has been hypothesized that in THA the combination of different implants from different manufacturers can lead to adverse effects. – A typical example of mix & match would be combining an acetabular cup and liner from one company with a stem and head from another. Bio-engineering commentary Acetabular bearing wear and friction depend on the combined materials and sizes. The head and socket diameters are slightly different, and from this difference the bearing clearance is defined. In particular with hard-on-hard bearings the clearance is an important parameter to promote mixed lubrication or fluid-film lubrication, ensuring low wear and friction. By combining components from different manufactures, the mode of lubrication might be altered, potentially leading to increased wear or pinching of the bearing. With hard-on-soft bearings the influence of the clearance is not as strong, as these bearing are generally not as sensitive regarding the mode of lubrication and furthermore the size of the polyethylene liner is requested by standardization (ISO 7206-2) to be slightly larger than the nominal bearing size. Consequently, pinching of the bearing is not expected even if a head and a polyethylene liner from different manufactures are combined. There is probably more concern with regard to tapers. Femoral heads are connected to the stem by a taper connection. The male taper or trunnion is the proximal part of the stem that is engineered to fit perfectly into the female taper on the underside of the femoral head (ball). This arrangement secures the head onto the stem. It is important to realize that modular tapers are not standardized and that they vary in terms of dimension and surface properties albeit they (i.e. the 12/14 taper) may be labelled the same. , As they can vary from manufacturer to manufacturer, it is agreed that combining a stem and head from different manufacturers should not be undertaken. They suggested that this could lead to increased weakness and a reduction in the stability of the construct. Summary It would seem that there are pros and cons to mixing and matching components from more than one manufacturer in a THA. The evidence suggests that reliable results in mix & match are only likely to be achieved when it is limited to combining cups and inserts from one manufacturer with stems and heads from another. Ceramics and metals from different manufacturers should never be mixed as materials coming from different fabricators may differ in their mixture. Careful thoughts based on available long-term results should be applied to any situation where mixing and matching head and stem is being considered. Cementing a polyethylene liner into a well-fixed acetabular component If removing the well-fixed metal back component of a modular acetabular component is thought to be contraindicated, cementing a new liner into the shell is an accepted procedure. , This option is particularly applicable when either a replica of the original liner is not available (either off-the-shelf or custom made) or when the locking mechanism is damaged. The shell size has to be adequate to accept a liner with a > 2 mm cement mantle around it and the operative technique does have to include scoring the inside of the metal shell in a spider web configuration to a depth of 1 mm to promote reliable bonding. Bensen et al have shown sufficient mechanical stability of cemented liners in an in vitro investigation, and several clinical studies report good intermediate to long-term results, although the dislocation rate has been reported to be as high as 17%. , , It has been suggested that the use of constrained liners may be an alternative to provide better stability. , However, it is likely that the liner dissociation rate would be increased due to the decreased impingement-free arc of motion, resulting in higher stress at the cement–implant interface. General recommendations Recommendation 7: As always, surgeons must be fully aware of the features of the components that they use off-label, must be appropriately trained and must audit their results. They should be aware of any off-label and on-label use of the product and the scientific basis behind its design. Surgeons should only use an off-label device after they have failed to find an on-label one that would be a suitable implant.
